subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 13 periods = 520 minutes
Total: 13 periods · 8h 40min

periods.activity_title: Tasting the Six Flavours of Ugadi Pachadi
periods.textbook_anchor: Mystery Masala — Students think about dishes they would include in a school food festival and make a list (p. 73)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustration of the Ugadi Pachadi stall (p. 73)

time_bands.activity: The teacher invites students to imagine walking into a school food festival and spotting an unusual stall called 'Mystery Masala'. She reads aloud the opening passage from Textbook p. 73, pausing to let students respond to the smells and tastes described. Students share one dish from their home that they would proudly bring to such a festival.

The teacher introduces Ugadi Pachadi and its six tastes — sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, and astringent — using the textbook description on p. 73. In pairs, students brainstorm what each taste reminds them of from their own kitchens, then share one example per taste with the class. The teacher writes the six taste words on the board in both English and any regional language familiar to the class.

Students open Textbook p. 73 and work individually on the Think and Write task: they list dishes they would include in a school food festival, thinking about which tastes those dishes represent. The teacher circulates, prompting students to name at least one dish for an unfamiliar taste.

A brief whole-class share: three or four students read out one dish each and say which taste it carries. The teacher draws out the idea that a festival with many different dishes naturally covers many different tastes — connecting to the Ayurvedic concept of Shad Rasa (six balanced tastes) mentioned in the textbook.

Students note in one sentence in their notebooks: 'Ugadi Pachadi contains all six tastes because a balanced meal should have all of them.' The teacher closes by asking: 'Can you think of a dish from your family that already has more than one of these tastes?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can recognise and name multiple distinct taste qualities present in a single food or dish.
periods.section_context: Ugadi Pachadi, six tastes (sweet/meetha, sour/khatta, salty/namkeen, pungent/teekha, bitter/karva, astringent/kasaila), Shad Rasa, school food festival dishes.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students whether anyone at home makes a dish that combines two or more of these tastes — this surfaces traditional family recipes naturally. Keep the share-out quick so every taste gets at least one example on the board before the writing task begins.

periods.textbook_anchor: Mystery Masala — Students write at least five ingredients or food items that match each of the six listed tastes (p. 74)

time_bands.activity: The teacher briefly recaps the six tastes introduced through Ugadi Pachadi, pointing to the taste words on the board. She asks one quick question: 'Which taste was hardest to think of an example for last time?' This surfaces the tastes — typically bitter and astringent — that need more attention in this activity.

Students open Textbook p. 74 and individually fill in the taste table: at least five ingredients or food items for each of the six taste categories. The teacher moves through the room, pausing beside students who are stuck on bitter or astringent to ask guiding questions about karela, methi, raw guava, or raw banana without naming the answer.

Students work in small groups on the Discuss task from Textbook p. 74: they identify food items in their combined lists that carry at least three different tastes — for example, tamarind chutney or a regional pickle. Each group nominates one such item and explains which three tastes they detect.

Groups share their multi-taste items. The teacher records one item per group on the board alongside its tastes. The class notices which tastes appear most often across the items and which are hardest to find — reinforcing why a variety of food is needed for a balanced Shad Rasa.

Students add one multi-taste item from today's discussion to their notebooks with the tastes it contains labelled. The teacher poses a closing prompt: 'Is there a spice or condiment at home that your family uses that might have more than one taste?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can classify food items by observable taste qualities and identify foods that carry multiple taste properties simultaneously.
periods.section_context: Six taste categories (sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, astringent), ingredients and food items mapped to each taste, multi-taste food items such as pickles and chutneys.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt students to think of preserved or fermented foods from their region — pickles, chutneys, fermented rice — which often carry three or more tastes, and draw out why families have made these for generations without necessarily knowing the Shad Rasa term.

periods.textbook_anchor: A Stall of 'Super Food' — Students find out more about a millet-based food prepared at their home (p. 75)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook image of the millet foods stall (p. 75)

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads the millet stall passage from Textbook p. 75 aloud, including the detail about the student whose grandmother ate jowar and bajra roti in winters and jau roti in summers. She pauses and asks: 'Has anyone in your family ever told you that certain foods are meant for a particular season?' Students share briefly in pairs.

The class builds a shared picture of the three millets introduced: jowar, bajra, and jau. For each one, students say what they know — colour, shape, how it is eaten at home, or what season. The teacher writes a simple three-column note on the board (millet name | what it looks like | when or how eaten at home) drawing from student responses.

Students work individually on the Find out task from Textbook p. 75: they recall and write down one millet-based food prepared at their home, noting the millet used, how it is cooked, and which family member usually makes it. Students who cannot think of a millet food at home are invited to write about one they have seen or heard of outside home.

Four or five students share their millet food with the class. The teacher notes patterns — winter use, festive use, everyday use — and draws out how this seasonal and community knowledge has been passed on without textbooks, through cooking and family tradition.
Students write one closing sentence: 'Millets like jowar, bajra, and jau are [one thing they now know about them].' The teacher asks: 'Why do you think millets are called a super food?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe traditional food practices linked to seasons and explain why a community food choice reflects both natural conditions and cultural knowledge.
periods.section_context: Millets (jowar, bajra, jau), seasonal eating practice (winter jowar/bajra roti, summer jau roti), millet-based foods prepared at home, nutritional richness of millets.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Invite students to name the person at home who cooks or knows about millets — grandmother, aunt, parent — to surface the idea that food knowledge is transmitted through people, not only textbooks, and that this is a valuable form of knowing.

periods.activity_title: Three Groups That Feed the Body
periods.textbook_anchor: How Does Food Help Us? — Students discuss why we need to eat different kinds of food items (p. 75)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook diagram or table of three food groups (p. 75–77)

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens with the Discuss question from Textbook p. 75: 'Why do we need to eat different kinds of food items?' She takes a few quick responses without correcting, letting student ideas surface. She then reads the section introduction, establishing that food does three jobs — giving energy, building the body, and protecting it.

The teacher presents the three food groups using the textbook (pp. 75–77): energy-giving foods (rice, wheat, potato, millets, ghee), body-building foods (pulses, legumes, milk, eggs, meat, fish), and protective foods (carrot, orange, spinach, amla). For each group, students say one food from their own meals that fits. The teacher records examples from students on the board under three columns.

Students open their notebooks and draw a simple three-column table headed Energy-Giving, Body-Building, and Protective. They list at least four foods they ate yesterday under the correct group. The teacher circulates, checking placements and asking students to explain their choice for one food.

The class addresses the second Discuss question from Textbook p. 77: 'What will happen if we eat food from a single group every day?' Students reason aloud — the teacher guides them toward the idea that each group does a different job and no single food can do all three jobs.

Students write one sentence summarising the key idea: 'No single food gives us everything our body needs, so we must eat from all three groups.' The teacher closes with: 'Which group do you think most people in your family eat least of?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can classify foods into functional groups based on what job they do in the body and explain why variety across groups is necessary.
periods.section_context: Three food groups: energy-giving (rice, wheat, potato, millets, ghee), body-building (pulses, legumes, milk, eggs, meat, fish), protective (carrot, orange, spinach, amla); need for dietary variety.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: When students list yesterday's meals, some may have eaten only one or two groups — treat this as data, not a problem, and use it to make the discussion concrete: 'Looking at your list, which job was your food doing most of yesterday?'

periods.activity_title: India's Thali — A Plate That Does It All
periods.textbook_anchor: How Does Food Help Us? — Students find out a food thali from their region and list its food items (p. 80)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook images of regional food thalis (pp. 75–80)

time_bands.activity: The teacher invites students to describe what a meal at their home looks like when the whole family eats together. She asks: 'Is everything served on one plate or in separate bowls? What does a full meal look like?' This surfaces the idea of the thali as a complete meal format before the textbook reading.

Students open Textbook pp. 75–80 and look at the images of regional thalis shown. The teacher reads the relevant passage explaining how India's regional thalis naturally combine foods from all three food groups. Students point out which items in the textbook thalis they recognise and which are new to them.

Students work individually on the Find out task from Textbook p. 80: they write the name of a food thali from their own region and list its food items. Then, beside each item, they write which food group it belongs to — energy-giving, body-building, or protective. The teacher helps students who are unsure of a food's classification.

Four or five students share their thali. The class listens for patterns: Does every thali have items from all three groups? Is there a group that appears in every thali? The teacher guides students to notice that the traditional thali is, in practice, a balanced food plate by design.

Students write: 'Our regional thali includes foods from [which groups they found].' The teacher closes with: 'Why do you think people arranged their meals this way long before anyone used the words energy-giving or body-building?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe how a regional food practice embodies nutritional balance and connect cultural food traditions to the concept of dietary variety.
periods.section_context: Regional food thalis from across India, food items within a thali classified into three food groups, cultural food diversity as balanced eating.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Students may describe thalis that are quite different from textbook examples — celebrate this variety and use it to reinforce that balance can be achieved through many different regional foods, not one single standard plate.

periods.textbook_anchor: Say 'No' to Junk Food — Students write junk food items they will avoid (p. 78)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustration of junk food items (p. 78)

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens Textbook p. 78 and reads the definition of junk food: food high in oil, salt, and sugar that is harmful when eaten regularly and in large quantities. She asks students to call out junk foods they have eaten in the past week — no judgement, just naming. The teacher notes responses on the board.

Students work on the Write tasks from Textbook p. 78: first, they name additional junk food items beyond those listed in the textbook; second, they write their own reason why junk food should be avoided. The teacher encourages personal language — 'I think …' — rather than copying a definition.

Whole-class discussion on the contrast between junk food and fresh home-cooked food. The teacher asks: 'When junk food is high in salt, what does that mean for the body? When it is low in nutrients, what is missing?' Students connect junk food's properties back to the three food groups studied earlier, identifying which groups junk food typically lacks.

Students individually complete the final Write task from Textbook p. 78: they list junk food items they personally will avoid and write one reason for each. The teacher asks them to be honest and specific — 'chips every day after school' rather than just 'chips' — so the list reflects real choices.

Students share one item from their avoidance list and one reason. The teacher affirms thoughtful reasoning. She closes with: 'Is there a healthier food from your home that gives you the same feeling of a snack — something crunchy, filling, or tasty?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify characteristics of unhealthy food choices and articulate specific personal reasons for avoiding them.
periods.section_context: Junk food definition (high oil, salt, sugar), examples (soft drinks, chips, bread pakoda, burgers, pizza, packaged food), contrast with home-cooked food, personal avoidance list.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: When students share what they will avoid, ask gently: 'What could you eat instead of that, that you also enjoy?' — this keeps the reflection forward-looking and practical rather than only restrictive.

periods.textbook_anchor: A Balanced Food Plate — Students create a food diary recording meals over a week and identify food groups missing from their daily routine (p. 79)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook diagram of the balanced food plate showing portion sizes by group (p. 79)

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens Textbook p. 79 and draws attention to the balanced plate diagram. She explains how the three sections are sized — protective foods are the largest, body-building foods next, energy-giving foods last. She asks: 'Does this match what your own plate usually looks like?' Students respond honestly.

The teacher explains the Food Diary activity from Textbook p. 79: students will record one full day's meals — breakfast, lunch, and dinner — in a table they draw in their notebooks. They set up the table now: columns for meal, food items eaten, food group, and a mark (circle for healthy, X for not healthy). The teacher models one row on the board with a sample meal.

Students fill in yesterday's or today's meals from memory — breakfast, lunch, and dinner or snacks. For each food item they write the food group, circle it if it is a healthy choice, and mark it with an X if it is not. The teacher circulates, helping students who are unsure of a food's classification or healthiness.

Students look at their completed day and identify: Which food group appears least? Which food group is missing entirely? They write one sentence naming the missing or underrepresented group and suggest one food from that group they could add to a future meal.
The teacher invites two or three students to share their finding. She closes with: 'If you were designing tomorrow's lunch to fix a missing group, what one food would you add and why?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can evaluate a day's meals against a balanced food framework and identify which nutritional group is missing or underrepresented.
periods.section_context: Balanced food plate with proportional sections (protective foods largest, then body-building, then energy-giving), food diary recording breakfast/lunch/dinner, healthy and unhealthy markers, identification of missing food groups.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Some students may feel uncomfortable if their meals look very unbalanced — frame the diary as information, not a grade: 'This is data about what we already eat, and we use data to make better choices, not to feel bad.'

periods.textbook_anchor: Water for Health — Students discuss water as an essential part of diet that aids digestion, keeps skin healthy, and removes waste (p. 80)

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: 'We have talked about food groups — where does water fit? Is it a food?' Students debate briefly. She then reads the Water for Health section from the textbook, establishing water's three jobs: aiding digestion, keeping skin and body healthy, and removing waste through urine, sweat, and faeces.

The class discusses each of water's three roles in turn. For each role, the teacher asks students to think of a sign they have noticed in their own body — e.g. dry lips when not drinking enough, darker urine, or skin feeling rough. Students share observations; the teacher connects each to the textbook explanation.

The teacher introduces the idea of water-rich foods from the textbook: watermelon and cucumber as examples of foods that also hydrate the body. Students brainstorm other water-rich foods they eat at home — fruits, vegetables, dal, soups. The teacher writes their suggestions on the board and asks: 'Do these foods feel hydrating when you eat them?'

Students write in their notebooks: three jobs of water in the body, and two water-rich foods from the discussion. They then write one personal habit they want to practise — 'I will drink water before going out to play' or similar — using their own words.

Two or three students share their personal water habit. The teacher closes with: 'In hot weather or after exercise, our body loses water faster — what do families in your home do to make sure everyone stays hydrated during summer?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can explain the role of water in body functioning and identify food sources that contribute to body hydration.
periods.section_context: Water's three roles (aiding digestion, keeping skin/body healthy, removing waste through urine/sweat/faeces), water-rich fruits (watermelon, cucumber), sufficient daily water intake as a health habit.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask about traditional summer drinks or practices at home — nimbu pani, buttermilk, raw mango drink, or clay pots for cooling water — to surface community knowledge about hydration that connects to the natural environment.

periods.activity_title: How Was This Cooked? Matching Food to Method
periods.textbook_anchor: Different Methods of Cooking — Students identify different cooking methods used for common food items from a given list (p. 81)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook list of food items with cooking methods (p. 81)

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: 'Think of the last thing you ate that was cooked. How was it cooked?' Students share — boiled, fried, baked, roasted. She introduces the six methods from the textbook: boiling, steaming, roasting, grilling, frying, and baking, writing each on the board. She also mentions that some foods — fruit chaat, vegetable salad — need no cooking at all.

Students open Textbook p. 81 and work on the Write task: they identify the cooking method for each food item in the textbook list, using the example given as a model. The teacher circulates and encourages students to take help from what they have seen at home — 'Have you watched this being made? How was it cooked?'

The teacher reads out each food item from the list and takes student responses. Where students disagree on the method, the class briefly discusses why — some foods can be cooked by more than one method, which is itself a useful discovery. The teacher adds the solar cooker fact from the textbook: it is an environment-friendly cooking method.

Students add two food items from their own home to the list in their notebook, name the cooking method used, and say who in their family usually cooks it that way. The teacher uses the Discuss questions from Textbook p. 82 informally: 'Do you help in cooking at home?' and 'Should all family members know how to cook?'

Students share responses to the second discuss question. The teacher closes with: 'Knowing how food is cooked also helps us know how healthy it is — which method do you think keeps the most nutrients in the food?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can match common foods to the method by which they are cooked and recognise that different cooking methods affect the nature of the food.
periods.section_context: Cooking methods (boiling, steaming, roasting, grilling, frying, baking), textbook list of food items matched to methods, uncooked foods (fruit chaat, vegetable salad), solar cooker as environment-friendly method.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: When students mention who cooks at home, use the discussion question about whether all family members should cook as an opportunity to surface equal participation in household work — the textbook raises this theme through the Discuss prompts on p. 82.

periods.activity_title: Food Collage — Sorting Into Three Groups
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students cut out pictures of food items and create a collage with three sections: energy-giving, body-building, and protective foods (p. 83)
materials: Old magazines, newspapers, or printed food images

time_bands.activity: The teacher explains the collage task from Textbook p. 83: students will create a three-section collage — one section for each food group — by cutting out food pictures from old magazines or newspapers. She distributes materials and shows how to divide the paper into three labelled sections.

Students cut out food images and sort them into the correct group section on their paper, gluing each picture down. For any food they are unsure of, they check Textbook pp. 75–77. The teacher circulates, asking students to explain a classification before they glue: 'Why is this a protective food?' Students who finish early add hand-drawn foods to any group that looks sparse.

Students do a gallery walk around the room, looking at two or three neighbours' collages. They identify one food they placed differently from their neighbour and discuss briefly why their placements differ. The teacher guides any genuine disagreements back to the textbook definition.

Students return to their seat and write the title of their collage and one sentence explaining why a balanced plate needs all three groups. The teacher collects the collages. She closes with: 'If you could add one food to the group that has the fewest pictures on your collage, what would it be?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can sort and represent food items across functional categories using a creative format and justify their classifications.
periods.section_context: Food collage with three sections (energy-giving, body-building, protective), food pictures cut from magazines/newspapers, classification of food items into groups.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Encourage students to include foods from their own region that may not appear in the textbook images — a regional green vegetable or a local pulse counts as much as a textbook example and makes the collage personally meaningful.

periods.activity_title: Reading the Label Before You Eat
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students check a packaged food label at home for expiry date and two main ingredients and explain why checking labels matters (p. 83)
materials: Any packaged food brought from home or a teacher-supplied sample label printed on paper

time_bands.activity: The teacher holds up a packaged food item (or a printed copy of a label) and asks: 'Before you eat this, what would you check?' Students guess — name, taste, colour, price. She then reads the label-check task from Textbook p. 83 and introduces the two things the textbook focuses on: expiry date and main ingredients.

Students who brought a packaged food from home take it out. Students without one pair with a neighbour who has one, or use a teacher-supplied sample label. Each student reads their label and notes in their notebook: the product name, the expiry date, and the first two ingredients listed. The teacher circulates, helping students find these items on labels with small print.

Students write their answer to the textbook question: 'Why is it important to check labels before buying or eating packaged food?' They write two or three sentences in their own words. The teacher then opens a brief class discussion — students share one reason each, and the teacher adds any reasons not yet mentioned: expired food can cause illness, ingredients tell us what is in the food, some ingredients may be unhealthy in large amounts.

The teacher connects label-checking back to junk food: 'If salt or sugar is the first ingredient listed, what does that tell you about the food?' Students reason from their earlier knowledge of junk food and the three food groups. This brief discussion reinforces inquiry rather than adding new content.

Students write one personal commitment in their notebook: 'From now I will check _____ on a label before I buy or eat it.' The teacher closes: 'Is there a packaged food at home that your family buys often? Would you check its label differently now?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can read a food product label to extract key information and explain why label-checking is a responsible food choice.
periods.section_context: Packaged food labels, expiry date, main ingredients listed on a label, reasons for checking labels before eating or buying.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: If students notice that a familiar snack has oil or sugar as its first ingredient, acknowledge this openly and ask what they might choose instead — the goal is informed decision-making, not anxiety about familiar foods.

periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students find and circle words related to food in a word-search grid (p. 84)

time_bands.activity: The teacher introduces the word-search activity from Textbook p. 84. She explains that every word hidden in the grid is a food-related term from the chapter. Before students start, she asks: 'How many food-related words can you name in thirty seconds?' Students call out words quickly — this activates chapter vocabulary.

Students open Textbook p. 84 and work individually to find and circle the words in the grid. The teacher allows this to be an unhurried, focused activity. Students who finish early are asked to write the meaning or food group of each word they found in the margin of their notebook.

The teacher calls out the words one by one and students confirm whether they found each one. For each word found, the teacher asks a quick question: 'Is this an energy-giving food, a body-building food, or a protective food?' or 'Which taste group does this belong to?' — connecting the vocabulary game back to chapter concepts.

Students use the words they have found to write five sentences in their notebooks — each sentence must use at least one word from the grid and say something true about food and health. The teacher circulates and encourages students to use chapter ideas rather than just listing the word alone.

Two or three students share a sentence each. The teacher closes with: 'Which word in the grid surprised you the most — either because you did not expect it or because you now know something new about it?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can locate and use food-related vocabulary in context, connecting terms to their nutritional or cultural meaning within the chapter.
periods.section_context: Word-search grid with food-related vocabulary from the chapter, food terms connected to food groups and tastes.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: When reviewing found words, linger on any term that students misclassify — a wrong food-group assignment during the review reveals a concept gap that can be addressed on the spot with a quick question rather than re-teaching.

periods.activity_title: From Taste to Plate — Bringing the Whole Chapter Together
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students organise a food festival at school with home-made food (p. 84)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook balanced plate diagram (p. 79) and food group table (pp. 75–77)

time_bands.activity: The teacher draws a large blank plate outline on the board and asks: 'If you were planning one meal that honours everything we have learned in this chapter — the six tastes, the three food groups, seasonal and traditional foods, enough water — what would you put on this plate?' Students call out suggestions; the teacher writes them inside the plate outline, labelling each with its food group and taste.

Students individually design their ideal balanced meal in their notebooks — a drawing or a labelled list — naming the food items, their food groups, and the tastes they carry. They also mark whether each item is home-cooked or packaged, and note whether they would check a label for any packaged item. The teacher circulates and asks students to explain one choice that reflects something from the chapter — a millet, a traditional dish, a water-rich food.

The teacher leads a whole-class reflection connecting chapter themes. She asks three questions in sequence: 'How does Shad Rasa — the six-taste principle — connect to the idea of a balanced plate?' then 'How does a regional thali show that people already knew about food balance before the terms energy-giving or protective existed?' then 'What would you now look for on a food label that you did not notice before?' Students respond, drawing on what they know.

Students write a personal food commitment in three parts: one food they will add to their meals (naming the group it belongs to), one food or habit they will reduce or avoid (and why), and one thing they will notice or check that they did not before. The teacher frames this as a choice, not a rule: 'This is what you have decided for yourself based on what you now know.'

The teacher closes by returning to the chapter's opening image of the food festival and the Mystery Masala stall. She asks: 'If you were running a stall at a food festival today, what one dish would you serve — and what would you want people to know about it?' Students share briefly. The teacher affirms that food is not only nutrition — it is culture, memory, and community.

periods.implied_lo: Students can integrate knowledge of food groups, taste qualities, traditional food practices, and healthy habits into a coherent personal food plan and articulate reasoned food choices.
periods.section_context: Synthesis of all chapter content: six tastes (Shad Rasa), Ugadi Pachadi, millets (jowar/bajra/jau), three food groups (energy-giving/body-building/protective), regional thalis, junk food avoidance, balanced food plate, water for health, cooking methods, food labels, food collage, word-search vocabulary.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: This unit may be the first time some students connect Shad Rasa to the three food groups — if the link surprises them, hold the moment: ask how ancient food traditions managed to encode nutritional balance without modern science, and let students reason about this.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can identify characteristics of unhealthy food choices and articulate specific personal reasons for avoiding them.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Junk food definition (high oil, salt, sugar), examples (soft drinks, chips, bread pakoda, burgers, pizza, packaged food), contrast with home-cooked food, personal avoidance list.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Say 'No' to Junk Food — Students write junk food items they will avoid (p. 78)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students name junk foods, write reasons for avoidance, and compile a personal list of junk food items they commit to reducing, connecting this to food group knowledge.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can evaluate a day's meals against a balanced food framework and identify which nutritional group is missing or underrepresented.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Balanced food plate with proportional sections (protective foods largest, then body-building, then energy-giving), food diary recording breakfast/lunch/dinner, healthy and unhealthy markers, identification of missing food groups.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: A Balanced Food Plate — Students create a food diary recording meals over a week and identify food groups missing from their daily routine (p. 79)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students design a food diary table, record one full day's meals, mark healthy and unhealthy items, and identify the food group missing from their day.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can explain the role of water in body functioning and identify food sources that contribute to body hydration.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Water's three roles (aiding digestion, keeping skin/body healthy, removing waste through urine/sweat/faeces), water-rich fruits (watermelon, cucumber), sufficient daily water intake as a health habit.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Water for Health — Students discuss water as an essential part of diet that aids digestion, keeps skin healthy, and removes waste (p. 80)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students discuss water's three body roles, brainstorm water-rich foods, and write a personal water habit they will practise.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can match common foods to the method by which they are cooked and recognise that different cooking methods affect the nature of the food.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Cooking methods (boiling, steaming, roasting, grilling, frying, baking), textbook list of food items matched to methods, uncooked foods (fruit chaat, vegetable salad), solar cooker as environment-friendly method.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Different Methods of Cooking — Students identify different cooking methods used for common food items from a given list (p. 81)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students match food items from the textbook list to their cooking method, add home examples, and discuss whether all family members should know how to cook.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can sort and represent food items across functional categories using a creative format and justify their classifications.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Food collage with three sections (energy-giving, body-building, protective), food pictures cut from magazines/newspapers, classification of food items into groups.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students cut out pictures of food items and create a collage with three sections: energy-giving, body-building, and protective foods (p. 83)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students create a three-section food collage by cutting and pasting food pictures into the correct group, then do a gallery walk and write a justification sentence.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can read a food product label to extract key information and explain why label-checking is a responsible food choice.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Packaged food labels, expiry date, main ingredients listed on a label, reasons for checking labels before eating or buying.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students check a packaged food label at home for expiry date and two main ingredients and explain why checking labels matters (p. 83)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students read a packaged food label, record the expiry date and main ingredients, and write their own explanation of why checking labels is important.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can locate and use food-related vocabulary in context, connecting terms to their nutritional or cultural meaning within the chapter.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Word-search grid with food-related vocabulary from the chapter, food terms connected to food groups and tastes.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students find and circle words related to food in a word-search grid (p. 84)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students complete the textbook word-search grid, classify each found word by food group or taste, and write five sentences using found vocabulary in meaningful context.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can integrate knowledge of food groups, taste qualities, traditional food practices, and healthy habits into a coherent personal food plan and articulate reasoned food choices.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Synthesis of all chapter content: six tastes (Shad Rasa), Ugadi Pachadi, millets (jowar/bajra/jau), three food groups (energy-giving/body-building/protective), regional thalis, junk food avoidance, balanced food plate, water for health, cooking methods, food labels, food collage, word-search vocabulary.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students organise a food festival at school with home-made food (p. 84)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students design an ideal balanced meal connecting all chapter themes, reflect on Shad Rasa and regional thalis, write a three-part personal food commitment, and share a dish they would serve at a food festival.

assessment_items.question_text: Ugadi Pachadi is a traditional dish that includes sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, and astringent tastes together. Why is a dish that contains all six tastes considered good for health according to Ayurveda?

options.label: A
options.text: Because a dish with six tastes means it was made from six different vegetables.

options.label: B
options.text: Because all six tastes together form a balanced combination known as Shad Rasa, which is considered complete for the body.

options.label: C
options.text: Because dishes with more tastes contain more salt and sugar, which give the body energy.

options.label: D
options.text: Because mixing many flavours makes food taste more interesting and enjoyable.

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is B. This item tests whether students understood the Ayurvedic Shad Rasa principle from the textbook reading, not merely that Ugadi Pachadi has multiple tastes.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can recognise and name multiple distinct taste qualities present in a single food or dish.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student understands that multiple tastes are present but confuses the cultural-health reason with mere sensory appeal — they have not engaged with the Shad Rasa explanation.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has conflated salt and sugar (energy sources) with the Shad Rasa principle — a cross-concept confusion between taste balance and nutrient function.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has misread 'six tastes' as 'six vegetables' — a surface reading error indicating the Shad Rasa concept was not retained from the textbook.

assessment_items.question_text: Look at the six taste categories: sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, and astringent. Name one food item that belongs to two or more of these taste categories at the same time, and write which tastes it carries.
expected_elements: Names a specific food item (e.g. a pickle, tamarind chutney, raw mango, amla, or any multi-taste food the student knows).
Correctly identifies at least two taste categories present in that food.
The two tastes named are plausible for the food item chosen.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any food item the student can plausibly support with two taste labels — region-specific pickles, chutneys, fermented foods, and raw fruits are all valid. A regionally varied answer is acceptable and correct: students from different states will name different foods, all of which may legitimately carry multiple tastes.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can classify food items by observable taste qualities and identify foods that carry multiple taste properties simultaneously.

competency.competency_text: Observes and describes cultural diversity in their immediate environment (food, clothing, games, different seasons, festivals related to harvest and sowing)

expected_elements: Names a specific food item (e.g. a pickle, tamarind chutney, raw mango, amla, or any multi-taste food the student knows).
Correctly identifies at least two taste categories present in that food.
The two tastes named are plausible for the food item chosen.

assessment_items.question_text: A student's grandmother eats jowar and bajra roti in winter and jau roti in summer. Why do you think she chooses different millets in different seasons? Write two reasons.
expected_elements: Recognises that different millets are suited to different seasons or climate conditions.
Connects seasonal food choice to either the body's needs in that season, the natural growing season of the millet, or traditional community knowledge about food.
At least one reason goes beyond 'because grandmother likes it' to reflect a seasonal or nutritional logic.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept reasoning that connects seasonal choice to warmth/cooling properties, to growing seasons, or to traditional community knowledge. A regionally varied answer is acceptable and correct — students from millet-growing regions may have detailed local knowledge that enriches the answer.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe traditional food practices linked to seasons and explain why a community food choice reflects both natural conditions and cultural knowledge.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

expected_elements: Recognises that different millets are suited to different seasons or climate conditions.
Connects seasonal food choice to either the body's needs in that season, the natural growing season of the millet, or traditional community knowledge about food.
At least one reason goes beyond 'because grandmother likes it' to reflect a seasonal or nutritional logic.

assessment_items.question_text: Ravi ate only dal and paneer for breakfast, lunch, and dinner every day for a week. Which problem is most likely to happen to his body?

options.label: A
options.text: His body will be well-protected because dal and paneer are healthy foods.

options.label: B
options.text: His body will grow very strong because he is eating body-building foods every day.

options.label: C
options.text: His body will have too much energy because dal and paneer give energy.

options.label: D
options.text: His body will miss energy-giving and protective nutrients because he ate from only one food group.

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is C. Dal and paneer are body-building foods; eating only from this group means energy-giving and protective foods are absent. Distractors test confusion between 'healthy food' and 'complete diet'.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can classify foods into functional groups based on what job they do in the body and explain why variety across groups is necessary.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has misclassified dal and paneer as energy-giving foods — a food group confusion that needs correction.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student equates 'healthy' with 'complete', not recognising that a food can be healthy but still leave other food groups unrepresented.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student correctly identifies dal and paneer as body-building but concludes this is sufficient, not recognising the need for all three groups.

assessment_items.question_text: A student says: 'A traditional food thali from my region already has everything the body needs — it is a naturally balanced meal.' Do you agree or disagree? Use what you know about the three food groups to explain your answer.
look_for: Takes a clear position (agree or disagree) and maintains it throughout.
Names at least two food groups and correctly identifies them as present or absent in a typical thali.
Connects a specific thali food item (rice, dal, sabzi, pickle, curd, roti) to a food group function.
Shows understanding that variety across groups — not just quantity — is what makes a meal balanced.
Writing is in the student's own words and goes beyond copying a textbook sentence.
assessment_items.annotation: A regionally varied answer is acceptable and correct — students may describe a thali from their own region, which may differ significantly from textbook examples. Accept any thali whose components the student can map to food groups, even if the thali is not named in the textbook. Award credit for reasoning, not for naming a specific thali.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe how a regional food practice embodies nutritional balance and connect cultural food traditions to the concept of dietary variety.

competency.competency_text: Observes and describes cultural diversity in their immediate environment (food, clothing, games, different seasons, festivals related to harvest and sowing)

look_for: Takes a clear position (agree or disagree) and maintains it throughout.
Names at least two food groups and correctly identifies them as present or absent in a typical thali.
Connects a specific thali food item (rice, dal, sabzi, pickle, curd, roti) to a food group function.
Shows understanding that variety across groups — not just quantity — is what makes a meal balanced.
Writing is in the student's own words and goes beyond copying a textbook sentence.

assessment_items.task: Think of one junk food item you or someone at home eats often. Write its name and three things about it that make it unhealthy. Then write one healthier food you could eat instead of it, and explain what good thing that food does for your body.
assessment_items.scaffold:
Junk food I am thinking about: ___________
Three things that make it unhealthy:
1.
2.
3.
A healthier food I could eat instead: ___________
What this food does for my body: ___________
format_of_output: Written response in the scaffold provided
Minimum three reasons for junk food being unhealthy
One healthy alternative with a reason
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any junk food item the student genuinely eats or has access to — chips, soft drinks, bread pakoda, biscuits, or local fried snacks are all valid. The healthy alternative should come from any of the three food groups. A regionally varied answer is acceptable and correct: students may name local snacks and local alternatives that are not in the textbook.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify characteristics of unhealthy food choices and articulate specific personal reasons for avoiding them.

competency.competency_text: Describes the basic safety needs and protection (health and hygiene, food, water, shelter, precautions, awareness of emergency situations, abuse, and unsafe situations) of humans, birds, and animals

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can apply the definition of junk food (high oil, salt, sugar; low in nutrients) to a real food item they know and identify a healthier alternative by connecting it to a food group function.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Look for specificity in the three reasons — a strong response names actual properties (too much oil, very high sugar, no vitamins) rather than vague statements ('it is bad for you'). The alternative food should be correctly linked to a food group.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: names a specific junk food, gives three distinct property-based reasons, names a healthy alternative and correctly explains its body function. Weak: gives only one reason or repeats the same idea three ways, names an alternative without explaining what it does.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who struggle with writing may draw the junk food and the healthy alternative with labels. Students who cannot think of a junk food they eat may choose a junk food they have seen advertised.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The scaffold structures the reasoning so students produce both critical analysis (why junk food is unhealthy) and constructive thinking (a better alternative), matching the R&A mode of the period.

assessment_items.question_text: Priya wrote down everything she ate yesterday. She had rice, dal, and roti for lunch, bread and butter for breakfast, and rice and sabzi for dinner. She did not eat any fruit or vegetable other than sabzi. Which food group is missing or very low in her day's meals? Name one food she could add and explain what that food will do for her body.
expected_elements: Correctly identifies protective foods (fruits and vegetables) as the missing or underrepresented group.
Names at least one specific fruit or vegetable as the food to add.
States one function of that food — protects the body, provides vitamins, or keeps the body healthy.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any fruit or vegetable as the suggested addition — regional fruits and vegetables are valid. The function stated should connect to the protective food group's role (vitamins, body protection) even if the student does not use those exact terms.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can evaluate a day's meals against a balanced food framework and identify which nutritional group is missing or underrepresented.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

expected_elements: Correctly identifies protective foods (fruits and vegetables) as the missing or underrepresented group.
Names at least one specific fruit or vegetable as the food to add.
States one function of that food — protects the body, provides vitamins, or keeps the body healthy.

assessment_items.question_text: Which of the following is the best description of what water does inside our body?

options.label: A
options.text: Water builds muscles and makes bones strong.

options.label: B
options.text: Water gives us energy to run and play.

options.label: C
options.text: Water helps digestion, keeps the body healthy, and removes waste.

options.label: D
options.text: Water protects us from heat by cooling the air around us.

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is C, directly drawn from the Water for Health section. Distractors test confusion between water's functions and the functions of food groups.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain the role of water in body functioning and identify food sources that contribute to body hydration.

competency.competency_text: Describes the basic safety needs and protection (health and hygiene, food, water, shelter, precautions, awareness of emergency situations, abuse, and unsafe situations) of humans, birds, and animals

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has confused water's role with the function of body-building foods — a cross-group confusion.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has confused water's role with the function of energy-giving foods — the most common cross-concept error in this chapter.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student knows water is connected to cooling or heat but has confused it with an external environmental function rather than an internal body function.

assessment_items.question_text: Look at the following foods: idli, tandoori chicken, fruit salad, and boiled eggs. For each food, write the cooking method used (or write 'no cooking needed' if it applies). Then write one food from your home that is cooked by the same method as idli.
expected_elements: Correctly identifies steaming as the method for idli.
Correctly identifies grilling or roasting as the method for tandoori chicken.
Correctly identifies 'no cooking needed' for fruit salad.
Correctly identifies boiling as the method for boiled eggs.
Names a home food that is also steamed, with the name being plausible.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept regional variants for the steamed home food — dhokla, modak, momos, patra, or any locally steamed item is correct. A regionally varied answer is acceptable and correct for the final part of the question.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can match common foods to the method by which they are cooked and recognise that different cooking methods affect the nature of the food.

expected_elements: Correctly identifies steaming as the method for idli.
Correctly identifies grilling or roasting as the method for tandoori chicken.
Correctly identifies 'no cooking needed' for fruit salad.
Correctly identifies boiling as the method for boiled eggs.
Names a home food that is also steamed, with the name being plausible.

assessment_items.task: Create a mini food collage using only drawings (no cutting or pasting needed). Draw at least six food items and arrange them into three labelled sections: Energy-Giving Foods, Body-Building Foods, and Protective Foods. For each section, write one sentence about what foods in that group do for your body.
assessment_items.scaffold:
Section 1 — Energy-Giving Foods
[Draw your foods here]
These foods help my body: ___________

Section 2 — Body-Building Foods
[Draw your foods here]
These foods help my body: ___________

Section 3 — Protective Foods
[Draw your foods here]
These foods help my body: ___________
format_of_output: Drawings of at least six food items distributed across three sections
Each section labelled with its food group name
One sentence per section explaining that group's function
assessment_items.annotation: Accept drawings of any recognisable food item — regional foods count equally with textbook examples. Check that each food is placed in the correct section; a misplaced food indicates a classification gap. The three function sentences need not be in textbook language — accept student phrasing that conveys the correct idea.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can sort and represent food items across functional categories using a creative format and justify their classifications.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can independently categorise food items into the three functional food groups and articulate each group's contribution to the body, using a visual and written format.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Check that the student has at least two foods in each section — a section with only one food suggests the student could not generate enough examples for that group. Sentences should say what the group does, not just name the group.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: six or more foods distributed across all three sections, each food correctly placed, sentences that state a specific body function. Weak: all foods in one section, foods in wrong sections, or sentences that simply repeat the group label.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who have difficulty drawing can write food names instead of drawing them. Students who need more support can label three pre-drawn plate outlines handed out by the teacher.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The drawing format allows students who struggle with extended writing to demonstrate classification skill; the sentence requirement ensures the creative output is grounded in conceptual understanding.

assessment_items.question_text: You pick up a packet of biscuits from your kitchen and check the label. You find that the expiry date was last month and the first two ingredients listed are sugar and refined flour. Write two things this label tells you and explain what you would do with this packet.
expected_elements: Identifies that the product is expired and should not be eaten.
Identifies that sugar and refined flour as the main ingredients indicate the biscuits are high in sugar and low in nutrients.
States a clear action — discard the packet, inform a family member, or not eat it — with a reason connected to the label information.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full marks for any response that correctly identifies both the expiry date problem and the ingredient concern, and proposes a reasonable action. The student does not need to use the exact term 'refined flour' — any phrasing that shows they noticed the main ingredient is a concern is acceptable.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can read a food product label to extract key information and explain why label-checking is a responsible food choice.

assessment_items.question_text: In the food word-search, a student finds the word AMLA. Which food group does amla belong to, and what job does it do in the body?

options.label: A
options.text: Body-building food — it builds muscles and repairs the body.

options.label: B
options.text: Energy-giving food — it gives the body fuel to move and work.

options.label: C
options.text: Junk food — it is sour, so it is not good to eat often.

options.label: D
options.text: Protective food — it helps protect the body and keep it healthy.

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is B. Amla is listed in the textbook as an example of a protective food. Distractor D is designed to catch students who confuse the sour taste of amla (from the Shad Rasa discussion) with junk food or unhealthy food.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can locate and use food-related vocabulary in context, connecting terms to their nutritional or cultural meaning within the chapter.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has misclassified amla as energy-giving, possibly confusing fruits generally with energy sources.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has misclassified amla as body-building, a common confusion between protective and body-building foods.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has confused amla's sour taste (from the Shad Rasa discussion) with junk food or unhealthy status — a cross-section confusion between taste and nutritional value.

assessment_items.question_text: A friend says: 'I eat rice, dal, sabzi, curd, fruit, and drink enough water every day — I think I already know everything I need to make good food choices.' Based on everything you have learned in this chapter, what would you add or change about your friend's thinking? Write your answer using at least three ideas from the chapter.
look_for: Affirms what is already good in the friend's eating — recognises the presence of all three food groups and water.
Adds at least one idea the friend has not considered — such as avoiding junk food, checking food labels, choosing a cooking method that preserves nutrients, or understanding the Shad Rasa principle.
Connects traditional food knowledge (millets, regional thali, Shad Rasa) to modern food group understanding.
Uses chapter vocabulary (food groups, balanced plate, junk food, Shad Rasa, protective/energy-giving/body-building) correctly in context.
The response shows synthesis — drawing from multiple sections of the chapter — rather than repeating one idea several times.
assessment_items.annotation: This synthesis item draws from the full chapter. Accept any three chapter-grounded ideas the student connects coherently. There is no single correct answer — reward breadth and quality of reasoning over exact vocabulary. A response that connects Shad Rasa to the balanced plate AND mentions junk food avoidance AND label-checking demonstrates strong synthesis.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can integrate knowledge of food groups, taste qualities, traditional food practices, and healthy habits into a coherent personal food plan and articulate reasoned food choices.
